population.note: City-proper figure is a recent-estimate midpoint (2020 census: 498,715); metro figure is the Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Alpharetta MSA, both pending Census reconciliation. fragmentationRatio left null: Atlanta metro is a nationally cited case study in municipal fragmentation via the 'cityhood movement' (Sandy Springs, Brookhaven, Dunwoody, Milton and others incorporating out of unincorporated Fulton/DeKalb County since 2005, largely to control local tax base and schools) but no single ratio has been computed for this guide -- flagged as a possible Field Notes follow-up rather than a number invented for this file.

recommendations.name: A Cappella Books
recommendations.note: Atlanta's most acclaimed general independent bookstore -- deep first-edition and signed-copy inventory, and one of the city's steadiest author-event calendars.

recommendations.name: Charis Books & More
recommendations.note: The South's oldest independent feminist bookstore, now partnered with Agnes Scott College; anchors Charis Circle, its nonprofit arm running queer, feminist, and social-justice programming.

recommendations.name: For Keeps Books
recommendations.note: Described as 'a cross between a store and a reading room,' focused on rare and classic Black publications, opened 2018 a few blocks from the Sweet Auburn corridor -- a living counterpoint to the district's erased commercial history.

recommendations.name: The Grim Reader Bookshop
recommendations.note: Horror, mystery, and occult specialist with a Southern Gothic aesthetic; started as a mobile shop out of a converted hearse before a planned Upper Westside storefront. Call ahead -- the brick-and-mortar opening was slated for summer 2026, right around this visit window.

recommendations.name: Offbeat Books
recommendations.note: Speculative fiction and unconventional nonfiction, hosting 'Weird Girl LitFic' book clubs, gaming meetups, and anti-imperialist reading groups -- as close as this guide's mandatory infoshop search came to finding a dedicated radical-political storefront in Atlanta proper.

recommendations.name: Criminal Records
recommendations.note: New and used vinyl heavy on indie, alternative, and underground genres, plus comics and merch -- the anchor record store of L5P's DIY-adjacent commercial strip.

recommendations.name: Disorder Vinyl
recommendations.note: Explicitly caters to punk, hardcore, indie, and alternative collectors with buy/sell/trade and band merch, near the MLK National Historical Park.

recommendations.name: Wax 'N' Facts
recommendations.note: Long-running used-vinyl mainstay across rock, rap, and country at genuinely affordable prices -- an L5P institution since the neighborhood's punk-scene heyday.

recommendations.name: Wuxtry Records
recommendations.note: Jazz, blues, indie, alt-rock, and hip-hop with a reputation for rare used finds; the Athens, GA sister store is where R.E.M.'s Peter Buck famously worked before forming the band.

recommendations.name: Moods Music
recommendations.note: Neo-soul, acid jazz, and hip-hop specialist rounding out the L5P record-store crawl with a genre focus the punk-leaning shops don't cover.

recommendations.name: Refuge Coffee Co.
recommendations.note: Nonprofit coffee shop and job-training program for refugees, based in Clarkston -- often called the most diverse square mile in America thanks to decades of refugee resettlement. A short drive out of downtown but the single strongest match in this guide for the leftist-politics/community-organizing interest.

recommendations.name: Land of a Thousand Hills Coffee
recommendations.note: Atlanta-based roaster built on direct-trade relationships with Rwandan coffee farmers -- a rare farmer-direct-sourcing story for a mid-size regional roaster rather than a boutique single-shop operation.

recommendations.name: Condesa Coffee
recommendations.note: Atlanta-grown specialty roaster with a plant-forward pastry case alongside dialed-in espresso.

recommendations.name: Dancing Goats Coffee Bar
recommendations.note: Batdorf & Bronson's Atlanta cafe inside Krog Street Market -- pair with a walk through the Krog Street Tunnel a block away.

recommendations.name: Aurora Coffee
recommendations.note: L5P coffeehouse institution with the neighborhood's scruffy, unhurried DIY character intact.

recommendations.name: Little Tart Bakeshop
recommendations.note: Small, quiet bakeshop known for large fruit tarts and savory quiches -- the fruit-forward pick of the bakery list.

recommendations.name: Star Provisions Market & Cafe
recommendations.note: Anne Quatrano's market-cafe, well known citywide for its giant black-and-white cookies, crispy chicken biscuit, and solid croissant program.

recommendations.name: Colette Bread & Bakeshop
recommendations.note: Fresh fruit- and vegetable-infused baking -- strawberry brioche tarts and shishito-pepper scones push past the standard croissant-and-muffin case.

recommendations.name: Alon's Bakery & Market
recommendations.note: Longtime Atlanta institution -- cinnamon twists, opera cakes, and full prepared-foods counters, a fixture since the 1990s.

recommendations.name: Hell Yeah Gluten Free
recommendations.note: The city's deepest gluten-free pastry case -- funfetti donuts and blueberry cheesecake pop tarts -- for anyone traveling with dietary restrictions.

recommendations.name: Luther Burger
recommendations.note: A burger served on a sliced, sugar-glazed donut (usually a Krispy Kreme) in place of a bun -- invented at Mulligan's Bar and named for R&B singer Luther Vandross. TasteAtlas's single Atlanta-exclusive dish entry.

recommendations.name: Fried Chicken & Southern Buffet -- Mary Mac's Tea Room
recommendations.note: Atlanta's 'dining room' since 1945 -- a Southern-cafeteria institution serving fried chicken, potlikker, and a table-side cup of tea (a house custom).

recommendations.name: Chili Dog & Frosted Orange -- The Varsity
recommendations.note: World's largest drive-in, open since 1928, famous for the counter-staff call-and-response ('What'll ya have?') and the Frosted Orange milkshake alongside the chili dog and onion rings.

recommendations.name: Frozen Fruit Salad & Chicken Salad -- Swan Coach House
recommendations.note: An old-Atlanta ladies-who-lunch institution on the Atlanta History Center grounds; the frozen fruit salad and chicken salad plate is a genuinely regional specialty, not a dish you'll find framed this way elsewhere.

recommendations.name: Georgia Peach Cobbler
recommendations.bestTimeOfDay: Late spring through summer, when Georgia peaches are in season
recommendations.note: Georgia is the Peach State for a reason; a proper peach cobbler at the tail end of a Southern-buffet meal is the fruit-interest pick for this category.

recommendations.name: Videri Chocolate Factory bars
recommendations.note: Atlanta bean-to-bar chocolate maker; shelf-stable bars travel and mail well.

recommendations.name: Beautiful Briny Sea pickles & bitters
recommendations.note: Atlanta-made pickled vegetables and cocktail bitters -- a jarred condiment gift with a genuinely local production story.

recommendations.name: Yo Mama's Foods sauces
recommendations.note: Atlanta-founded jarred pasta sauce and mustard company -- shelf-stable, easy to mail.

recommendations.name: Bee Downtown local honey
recommendations.note: Bee Downtown places managed hives on corporate rooftops (Delta's Atlanta HQ among them) and sells the resulting honey at retail -- a direct hit for the bees interest.

recommendations.name: ASW Distillery Fiddler Bourbon
recommendations.note: Atlanta craft distillery's flagship bourbon and rye line -- bottled, giftable, and tied to an in-city tasting-room visit (see Category 10-adjacent whiskey note).

recommendations.name: Sweet Auburn Historic District & MLK National Historical Park

citedFrom.label: Wikipedia -- Sweet Auburn; National Park Service

recommendations.note: Once 'the richest Negro street in the world' (Fortune, 1956); Dr. King's birth home, Ebenezer Baptist Church, and his tomb anchor the district, which the Downtown Connector freeway split in half in the mid-20th century. This guide's cross-trip thread anchor.

recommendations.name: Doll's Head Trail
recommendations.note: A folk-art trail built from salvaged doll parts, bones, and industrial debris found in and around the wetland -- genuine outsider art, unofficial and ever-changing.

recommendations.name: Oakland Cemetery
recommendations.note: Atlanta's oldest public park and 48-acre Victorian cemetery; Margaret Mitchell and golfer Bobby Jones are buried here. The 'Capturing the Spirit of Oakland' theatrical Halloween tours are a 20-plus-year tradition, though outside a May visit window.

recommendations.name: Krog Street Tunnel
recommendations.note: A constantly repainted street-art tunnel connecting Cabbagetown to Inman Park/Reynoldstown -- appears in Baby Driver and is a working canvas rather than a museum piece, so it looks different every visit.

recommendations.name: Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area (Cochran Shoals)
recommendations.note: A chain of river-corridor park units through metro Atlanta with hiking, shoals swimming, and summer tubing -- the natural-attraction balance-rule pick, and genuinely close enough to be a half-day trip rather than a detour.

recommendations.name: Trap Music Museum
recommendations.note: Billed as the world's first hip-hop museum, founded out of T.I.'s trap-music roots; recognized by National Geographic as one of the best musical landmarks in the Deep South. Not a core-interest match but a genuinely distinctive, only-in-Atlanta pop-culture stop.

recommendations.name: National Center for Civil and Human Rights
recommendations.note: Pairs the American civil rights movement with a global human-rights gallery; the lunch-counter simulation exhibit is the standout for the political-history thread, and it sits a short walk from the World of Coca-Cola if you want the postcard stop too.

recommendations.name: The Masquerade
recommendations.note: Atlanta's best-known rock club since 1989, split into three named rooms (Heaven, Hell, Purgatory) that let it run multiple bills a night across metal, punk, and touring indie acts.

Confirmed active DIY-leaning punk/metal/hardcore booking (EYEHATEGOD, Voivod, Kylesa, Profanatica have all played recently) inside a small East Atlanta Village room -- the closest match in this guide to a genuine underground show space.

recommendations.name: Star Community Bar
recommendations.note: L5P dive institution since the early '90s, complete with an Elvis shrine in the basement chapel -- rockabilly, garage, and punk-adjacent bookings in the neighborhood that produced Black Lips and the Nu-South garage scene.

recommendations.name: The Earl
recommendations.note: Restaurant-venue combo that's been an indie/punk mainstay since the early 2000s, a short walk from 529 -- the two anchor an East Atlanta Village show-going night.

recommendations.name: Boggs Social & Supply
recommendations.note: Community bar and DIY show space inside Cabbagetown, the historic mill-village neighborhood next to Oakland Cemetery -- low-key and community-run rather than a booking-agency room.

recommendations.name: Junkman's Daughter
recommendations.note: A cavernous vintage/retro/oddity emporium and L5P landmark since the 1980s -- the single best browse-for-a-weird-gift stop in the city.

recommendations.name: Paris on Ponce
recommendations.note: A sprawling antiques-and-oddities warehouse that doubles as an event space; browsing here is closer to an Atlas Obscura outing than a shopping trip.

recommendations.name: Young Blood Boutique
recommendations.note: Local-artist gallery-shop in L5P selling prints, apparel, and small goods made by Atlanta makers rather than mass-market tourist stock.

recommendations.name: Trap Music Museum gift shop
recommendations.note: Museum-branded apparel and merch that reads as a genuinely Atlanta-specific souvenir rather than a generic tourist tee.

recommendations.name: MLK National Historical Park bookstore & gift shop
recommendations.bestTimeOfDay: Paired with the Sweet Auburn visit
recommendations.note: Civil-rights-history postcards, prints, and books that make a more meaningful souvenir than a generic magnet, sold on-site at the historical park.

recommendations.name: Freeside Atlanta
recommendations.estCost: Membership-based; open-house nights typically free to visit
recommendations.bestTimeOfDay: Check calendar for open build nights
recommendations.note: Self-described as the largest hackerspace on the East Coast -- roughly 5,500 sq ft with a wood shop, metal shop, CNC router, CO2 laser cutter, and a 16-student classroom. Confirmed active via Hackaday coverage.

recommendations.name: Decatur Makers
recommendations.note: Nonprofit community makerspace with a tool library and regular classes -- a more approachable, less industrial counterpart to Freeside for a short-notice visit.

recommendations.name: Georgia Tech Invention Studio
recommendations.note: One of the largest student-run makerspaces in the country -- 3D printing, laser cutting, electronics benches -- but it's primarily built for enrolled students, so public/visitor access needs confirming ahead of time rather than assuming a walk-in tour.

recommendations.name: ASW Distillery tour & tasting
recommendations.note: Not electronics, but included here as the whiskey/bourbon-and-craft-production stop this itinerary would otherwise miss -- three Atlanta tasting rooms making Fiddler Bourbon, Resurgens Rye, and other in-house spirits.

filmedHere.title: Black Panther
filmedHere.visitNote: A real, still-skateable public skatepark on the BeltLine that doubled for a Wakandan chase sequence -- walkable from Sweet Auburn. Core Wakanda soundstages were built here, roughly 30 miles south of downtown -- not walkable from the city, but the reason 'Atlanta' films read as a production hub rather than a backdrop.

filmedHere.title: Baby Driver
filmedHere.visitNote: The opening car chase runs through real downtown Atlanta streets; the Krog Street Tunnel area (Cabbagetown/Reynoldstown) appears in later sequences and is freely walkable, still covered in rotating street art.

filmedHere.title: The Walking Dead
filmedHere.visitNote: The pilot's iconic image of Rick riding a horse into an abandoned downtown Atlanta was shot on real closed downtown streets. Ongoing series production largely moved about 35 miles south to Senoia, GA (the fictional 'Woodbury'), which is not Atlanta proper -- a common point of confusion for visitors chasing filming locations.

filmedHere.title: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire
filmedHere.visitNote: Capitol and arena sequences used the speedway and other metro locations well outside the walkable downtown core.

bornHere.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
bornHere.note: Born and raised on Auburn Avenue; the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park (birth home, Ebenezer Baptist Church, his tomb) anchors the neighborhood and this guide's analytical thread.

bornHere.name: Killer Mike (Michael Render)
bornHere.note: Run the Jewels rapper and outspoken leftist political commentator (police reform, Black-owned business advocacy); co-owns SWAG Shop barbershop in the Old Fourth Ward, blocks from Sweet Auburn.

bornHere.name: Margaret Mitchell
bornHere.note: Author of Gone with the Wind, buried at Oakland Cemetery. Worth naming honestly: the novel is a Lost Cause romance of the Confederacy, not a text this guide is holding up uncritically -- included because her grave and the book's cultural footprint are inescapably part of Atlanta's literary landscape.
